b2plus-inca.title: As Soon As / When: -(y)IncA
b2plus-inca.explanation: -(y)IncA is a converb meaning 'as soon as / when,' more compact than -DIğI zaman and often implying the second action follows immediately: 'Eve varınca seni ararım' (As soon as I get home, I'll call you). Like -ArAk, it uses simple 2-way harmony and attaches to every verb with no exceptions, regardless of aorist irregularity.
b2plus-inca.fact: -(y)IncA describes a single triggering moment, not a repeated pattern -- for 'every time X happens,' Turkish instead reaches for -DIkçA, a related but distinct suffix.

dialogue.en: When will you let me know?
As soon as I decide, I'll tell you right away.

b2plus-dikca.title: As Long As / The More / Every Time: -DIkçA
b2plus-dikca.explanation: -DIkçA describes an action that continues alongside another, growing or repeating in step with it: 'Çalıştıkça gelişiyorum' (The more I work, the more I develop). It overlaps with ne kadar...o kadar but is more compact, a single clause instead of two parallel ones, and also covers 'every time X happens': 'Onu gördükçe gülümserim' (Every time I see him, I smile).
b2plus-dikca.fact: -DIkçA and -DIğIndA both build on the -DIk participle, but they mean different things: -DIğIndA marks a single moment ('when X happened'), while -DIkçA marks a repeated or ongoing correlation ('the more/every time X').

dialogue.en: How do you find this city?
The more I explore it, the more I love it.

b2plus-madikca.title: Unless / As Long As...Not: -mAdIkçA
b2plus-madikca.explanation: Negate -DIkçA and you get 'unless / as long as X doesn't happen': 'Çalışmadıkça başaramazsın' (Unless you work, you won't succeed). It's a strong, almost proverbial way to state a necessary condition, more forceful than a plain -mAzsA conditional.
b2plus-madikca.fact: -mAdIkçA pairs naturally with a negative result too, reinforcing the warning: 'Konuşmadıkça anlaşamayız' (Unless we talk, we can't understand each other) — both halves being negative is normal here, not a double-negative mistake.

dialogue.en: How will we solve this problem?
Unless we talk, we can't solve it.

b2plus-since.title: Since: -DIğIndAn beri
b2plus-since.explanation: To say 'ever since X happened,' attach the ablative case to the -DIk clause you already know, then follow with beri: 'Buraya geldiğimden beri çok değiştim' (Since I came here, I've changed a lot). With a simple noun or time expression, beri also attaches directly: 'İki yıldan beri burada yaşıyorum' (I've been living here for two years).
b2plus-since.fact: With beri, Turkish typically uses the PRESENT tense (-Iyor) even though English uses a present perfect ('have been living') — the action is framed as still ongoing right now, not as a completed block of time.

dialogue.en: Since when have you been living here?
I've been here since I finished university.

b2plus-ma-subject.title: Verbs as Subjects: -mAk and -mA + Possessive
b2plus-ma-subject.pattern: verb-mAk (bare infinitive as subject); verb-mA + possessive (naming whose action)
b2plus-ma-subject.explanation: You've used -mAk as the dictionary/infinitive form and -mA in object clauses (istemek, hoşlanmak). -mAk can also stand as the SUBJECT of a sentence: 'Erken kalkmak zor' (Getting up early is hard). When you need to specify WHOSE action, switch to -mA + possessive instead: 'Onun erken kalkması zor' (His getting up early is hard) — -mAk stays generic and impersonal, -mA + possessive names the doer.
b2plus-ma-subject.fact: Bare -mAk can only be a subject or sit right before a small set of light verbs (istemek, gerekmek); once you need a possessive suffix, case ending, or plural, Turkish always switches to the -mA nominal, never adds those directly onto -mAk.

dialogue.en: What do you think is the hardest thing?

b2plus-particles.title: Discourse Particles: zaten, üstelik, hatta, işte, tabii
b2plus-particles.pattern: particle at the start or middle of a sentence
b2plus-particles.explanation: zaten ('already, anyway, as it is') reinforces that something was already true, often justifying a point: 'Zaten geç kalmıştım' (I was already late anyway). üstelik ('moreover, on top of that') piles on an extra fact: 'Pahalıydı, üstelik kalitesizdi' (It was expensive, and on top of that, low quality). hatta ('even, in fact') introduces a stronger example, similar to bile but working as a connector between clauses: 'Herkes geldi, hatta patron bile geldi' (Everyone came, even the boss came). işte ('there, right there / that's exactly it') points at something or confirms a statement emphatically: 'İşte bu!' (That's exactly it!). tabii ('of course, naturally') signals obviousness or agreement: 'Tabii ki gelirim' (Of course I'll come).
b2plus-particles.fact: These five particles are some of the most frequent words in spoken Turkish, but they appear far less densely in formal writing — overusing them in writing can sound too casual, while underusing them in speech can make a learner sound stiff or overly formal.

dialogue.en: Why did you leave so early?

dialogue.tr: Zaten yorgundum, üstelik yarın erken kalkmam gerekiyordu.
dialogue.en: I was already tired, and on top of that, I had to get up early tomorrow.

b2plus-mis-hearsay.title: Hearsay and Rumor: Extended -mIş
b2plus-mis-hearsay.pattern: verb + -mIş (+ -mIş chains); duyduğuma göre / söylentiye göre + -mIş clause
b2plus-mis-hearsay.explanation: You've used -mIş for evidential/inferential past (things you didn't witness directly but conclude from evidence). The same suffix is also Turkish's main way to report RUMOR or hearsay — things you only know because someone told you, with no personal confirmation: 'Yarın toplantı iptal olmuşmuş' (Apparently the meeting has been canceled, so I've heard). Framing phrases like duyduğuma göre (from what I've heard) or söylentiye göre (according to rumor) make the secondhand source explicit.
b2plus-mis-hearsay.fact: Doubling -mIş (olmuşmuş, gelmişmiş) specifically marks something you heard SECONDHAND, distinct from a single -mIş, which can be your own inference from evidence you saw yourself — the double marks 'I'm just repeating what I was told,' often with a hint of skepticism or distance.

dialogue.tr: Duydun mu, yeni bir şube açılıyormuş.
dialogue.en: Did you hear, apparently a new branch is opening.
Really? Who did you hear it from?

b2plus-postpositions-extended.title: Extended Postpositions: itibaren, boyunca, süresince, karşı, ait
b2plus-postpositions-extended.pattern: -DAn itibaren (starting from); noun + boyunca/süresince (throughout); noun + -A karşı (against/toward); noun + -A ait (belonging to)
b2plus-postpositions-extended.explanation: itibaren follows the ablative and means 'starting from': 'Yarından itibaren yeni programa geçiyoruz' (Starting from tomorrow, we're switching to the new program). boyunca and süresince follow a plain noun and mean 'throughout/during the whole of': 'Tatil boyunca çalıştım' (I worked throughout the vacation) — süresince is more formal/precise about a bounded duration. karşı follows the dative and means 'against, toward' (both a physical direction and an attitude): 'Bu karara karşıyım' (I'm against this decision). ait follows the dative and means 'belonging to': 'Bu kitap bana ait' (This book belongs to me).
b2plus-postpositions-extended.fact: karşı can flip between a neutral direction ('rüzgara karşı yürüdük,' we walked against/into the wind) and a strong opinion ('şiddete karşıyım,' I'm against violence) — context, not the word itself, tells you which meaning is active.
